title: Best Packaging and Label Designers (2026): How to Hire One
description: How to hire a packaging or label designer: what the package should include, how to brief it, what drives the price and the red flags.
intro: Packaging has to sell on a shelf or a screen, carry the right legal information, and print correctly on the first run. Most costly mistakes happen at the printer: wrong dimensions, missing bleed, or text that is too small to read. This guide helps you order a design that is ready to print.

faq.q: What is a dieline and do I need one?
faq.a: A dieline is the flat outline of your box, bag or label with folds and cuts marked. Your printer or packaging supplier usually provides it. Designing without the correct dieline is the most common reason packaging fails to print properly.

faq.q: Which files will the printer need?
faq.a: Usually a print-ready PDF or vector file in CMYK or with specified spot colors, with bleed and the dieline on a separate layer. Ask your printer for their exact file requirements and pass them to the designer.

faq.q: Who is responsible for the legal text?
faq.a: You are. The designer places the text you provide, such as ingredients, warnings, barcodes and required symbols. Requirements depend on the product and country, so check the rules that apply to you.
Many designers include a 3D mockup so you can see the package from all sides. It is useful for approvals and online listings, but always print a physical proof before a large run.
Confirm it in writing. Ask for full rights to the final design and the source files, so you can reprint or adapt it with another designer later.
